sources.title: Your questions about Apple HomeView’s audio, answered
passages: Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.) The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent.
After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker.
Here are the answers to all your burning questions.
Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle.
You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods.
For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return.
Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV.

This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).

extraction.body: After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling. You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView: [Video: Apple HomeView Smart Speaker Audio Testing] The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.) The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell. Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound? [Image: Two HomeViews can’t be paired for stereo sound, as the HomePod Minis can. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms. If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly. For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker. So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music. Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps). In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi.

I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter!
You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods.
Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen.
Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone.
YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView.
But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser.
As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.
However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers.
I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.
For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return.
Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV.
The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen.
If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.
So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify.

I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.
Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps?
Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform.

This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).
In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi.

passages: Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week.

The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend.

Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

extraction.body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future. The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

extraction.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. How it started Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?” Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices. In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotaku that the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.” The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want? With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solid on the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list. What happens next The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. sources.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
passages: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said.
“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default.
Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

extraction.body: Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk. “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch. That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers. But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.” Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China. After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap. And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said. Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.” What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others. “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch. Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail. Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls. “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.” The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said. “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.” Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information. Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?” It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company. Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said. “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. sources.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
passages: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

extraction.body: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement . “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added. The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen). The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position. The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government. The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. extraction.body: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion. Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California. Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations. Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption. Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI. “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.” Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.
Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

sources.body: From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

extraction.body: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier. From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace. If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward. The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed. You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording. The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages. Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk. Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table. If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year). Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier. The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes. Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas. Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries. If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you. Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls. The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls. Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday. Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits. The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window. passages: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.
From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.
You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.
The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.
If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).

Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.

The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.
Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

extraction.body: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return. Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.) Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China. What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down. A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027. Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country. It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting. So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way. Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him. It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.” So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen. Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks. Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there. Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that. Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

sources.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
passages: If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them.
I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong.
If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011.

“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero.
Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.
Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate.
This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator.
A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia!
But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.

extraction.body: We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception. Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor. On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains. Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his. “The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied. Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped. So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account. “Ha, yes, that’s me,” he replied. So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd. You can contact or verify outreach from Amanda by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at @amanda.100 on Signal. sources.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
passages: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list.
Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.

Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects.
Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore.

Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground.
And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country.
Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction.
Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery.

As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general.
And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

extraction.body: Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most. (Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.) As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945. Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel. Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero . Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers. It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play. (WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.) Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.) Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution. Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb. Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.
