extraction.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. How it started Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?” Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices. In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotaku that the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.” The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want? With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solid on the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list. What happens next The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

sources.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
passages: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said.
“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default.
Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default.
Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

extraction.body: Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk. “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch. That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers. But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.” Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China. After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap. And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said. Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.” What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others. “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch. Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail. Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls. “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.” The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said. “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.” Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information. Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?” It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company. Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said. “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. integrityPreflight.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China

sources.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
passages: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

extraction.body: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement . “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added. The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen). The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position. The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government. The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

sources.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
passages: “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step.
It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents.

In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year.
Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space.
It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

passages: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website .
One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”
If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies.

sources.title: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
passages: From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
sources.body: From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

extraction.body: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier. From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace. If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward. The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed. You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording. The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages. Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk. Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table. If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year). Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier. The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes. Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas. Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries. If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you. Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls. The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls. Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday. Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits. The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window. extraction.body: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier. From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace. If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward. The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed. You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording. The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages. Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk. Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table. If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year). Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier. The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes. Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas. Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries. If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you. Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls. The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls. Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday. Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits. The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window. integrityPreflight.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd

sources.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
passages: If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them.
I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong.
If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011.

“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero.
Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.
Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate.
This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator.
A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia!
But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.

extraction.body: We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception. Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor. On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. candidates.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels

integrityPreflight.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels

sources.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
passages: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list.
Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.

Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects.
Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore.

Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film. Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

passages: Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.
Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act.

extraction.body: Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels. Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

passages: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

According to NPR: > Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan. According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: > On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

extraction.body: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations. According to NPR: > Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan. According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: > On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

extraction.body: Friday, it was reported that both the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI were hacked. In reporting on the FBI hack, CNN noted that this is the second such attack on the agency in the last few months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state, and local law enforcement use to share information, including warrants and missing persons. According to Reuters: > While the payments ​database is the known extent ​of the intrusion so far, the former ‌officials ⁠warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety ​data and ​research on ⁠animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. The breaches come following a week of major outages across several sectors, including at the FAA and NSA, which the government has sought to reassure the public were not the result of a cyberattack. President Trump suggested that the breach of the FBI might not be an entirely bad thing, telling Fox News that, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” and “wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?” referring to investigations into his ties to Russia. candidates.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday

integrityPreflight.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday

sources.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
passages: Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday.
You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos.
A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads.
We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member.
If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app.
It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud.

You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself.
Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up.

extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

relevantPassages.text: We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders.

I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public.
But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

extraction.body: If you’re looking for a new pair of earbuds, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are on sale for $129.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart right now. The microphone does an impressive job cutting out background noise, and my colleague John Higgins praised the Liberty 5 Pro for filtering out emergency vehicles, arborists cutting tree branches, and even loud children. The active noise cancellation is excellent, which helps when you’re trying to hear someone on the other end of the phone whose earbuds aren’t as clear as yours. The charging case also features a handy 0.96-inch screen, so you can adjust the ANC and sound profile on the fly. Read our Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro review.

extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com . To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote: The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models. The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com .

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.
